title: A good eye (Avot 2:11)
hook: an evil eye, the bad urge and hatred of people drive a person out of the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvah: Rabbi Eliezer said repent one day before you die, and nobody knows the day. Your line was repent today.

A friend posts a photo of her new house. You tap the heart. And somewhere under the heart, there's a small, sour feeling. Why her? She didn't even work that hard. You'd never say it out loud. But you felt it. Everybody has. Two days ago, Rabbi Eliezer's answer to the teacher's question was a good eye. Today another of those five students, Rabbi Joshua, describes the opposite. And he says it doesn't just spoil your mood. It drives you out of the world.
screen: `THE HEART UNDER THE PHOTO.` → `A SMALL, SOUR FEELING.` → `RABBI JOSHUA'S WARNING.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Joshua says three things drive a person out of the world: an evil eye, the bad urge, and hatred of people. The evil eye isn't what you might think. In the Mishnah, it isn't a curse or a spell. It's a way of looking: a stingy, begrudging eye, the eye that sees someone else's good fortune and wishes, a little, that they didn't have it. A good eye is the opposite: glad when others do well, and giving freely. Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye is blessed, because he shares his bread with the poor. The Hebrew there is tov ayin, literally good of eye. Then the bad urge, the yetzer hara, the pull toward the selfish thing. And hatred of people, of anyone at all. Why would these drive you out of the world? Commentators give several answers. One is simple: they make you miserable, and wear your life down. Another is that they cut you off. If every friend's good news stings, you slowly stop being able to be with people. You end up alone in a crowd. The good eye opens the world back up: when you can be glad for others, their joy becomes a little bit yours. And that closes a week of Hillel and his heirs: you haven't been there, be a mensch, harm comes back, more isn't more, a good heart, repent today, and now, a good eye.
screen: `THREE THINGS DRIVE YOU OUT.` · `THE EVIL EYE: A BEGRUDGING LOOK.` · `TOV AYIN: GOOD OF EYE.` · `ALONE IN A CROWD, OR GLAD.` · then, large: `A GOOD EYE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose good news stung a little, a promotion, a trip, a new relationship, and don't pretend the sting isn't there. Then slowly picture them enjoying what they have, their face, their relief, and wish it for them sincerely, with no but at the end. If it's hard, start small, and try again.
Ayin tovah. A good eye, a generous way of seeing: glad when others do well, the opposite of the begrudging eye that drives a person out of the world.
Your line: glad when others do well. Tov ayin, good of eye. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Jewish ethics, ayin tovah, a good eye, means generosity and gladness at others' good fortune, and it is often taught alongside the laws of giving.

chat.says: What's an evil eye in the Mishnah? Is it like a curse?
options: Not a curse. It's a begrudging way of seeing someone else's good fortune.
A tired, unfocused eye that keeps a person from noticing what's going on.
Looking at your own faults so much that you forget to notice others.
chat.meaning: In the Mishnah the evil eye is a stingy, begrudging way of looking. A good eye is glad when others do well, and gives freely.

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:11 common, 2:16 in some editions.
Proverbs 22:9 is now paraphrased (see audit note).

The script says the Mishnah's evil eye is a way of looking, not a curse. Jewish folk tradition does also know the evil eye as a harmful gaze (and some Talmudic passages treat it that way); a Keeper may want a note acknowledging both.
Explanations of 'drive out of the world' (shortens life; isolates) are general summaries of commentators; confirm.
